text: The printer had borrowed against the press, the type and the lease on the shop, and for two years his almanac sold out before Christmas. In the third year, the bishop read it, and the press went to the lender.
strengths: a long sentence of rising fortune answered by a shorter one that holds the fall
the bishop's verdict is never stated, and the lost press says it for him
the debt planted in the first clause is paid off in the last
weaknesses: the listener has to supply the ban and the lost sales, so the next block should give the bishop's objection from the record
a reversal this compressed works once in a sequence, not as a house habit
spokenRhythm: One long breath that piles up debt and success, then a fifteen-word sentence that turns on its comma, the bishop on one side and the lender on the other.
narrativeFunction: Turns a printing success story into censorship and ruin, and opens a section on what the church could do to a press.
whyItWorks: The first sentence does two jobs at once, building the success and quietly pledging everything the printer owns. The second names a reader and a consequence and leaves out the step between them, so the listener works out the ban alone. It resolves the story instead of teasing it, and the dryness lies in what the narrator declines to say.

text: The river rose on Monday. On Tuesday it took the footbridge. On Wednesday it reached the wheel pit, and the paper mill stopped. By Thursday the owners had bought every sandbag in the county, which came, in the end, to about sixty.
strengths: short full sentences used once, for escalation, each with a subject and a verb
each sentence is a little longer than the one before, so the rhythm swells with the water
the dry release keeps the escalation from becoming melodrama
weaknesses: the day-by-day openings are an audible device and belong in one passage of a film, not several
the first three sentences are generic flood writing until the sandbag figure arrives
spokenRhythm: Five words, then six, then twelve, then a nineteen-word sentence that relaxes into a dry aside.
narrativeFunction: Builds the pressure of a flood on a mill, then releases it with an absurd and specific detail.
whyItWorks: These are short sentences, not fragments. Each has a subject and a verb and moves the water a step further, and the lengths grow as the danger grows, so the rhythm follows the flood. The last sentence breaks the pattern with a figure that is almost comic, which tells the listener the narrator is in control of the device rather than driven by it. Unlike a bare run of short lines, it resolves instead of stopping on the drumbeat.

text: On the coast, salt was cheap. Every town it passed through on the way inland charged a toll at the gate, and every toll was added to the price, so by the time a sack reached the hill country it had paid for its journey several times over. A labourer's family there could spend a fortnight's wages on the salt it needed for a year.
strengths: a long sentence the ear can follow because each clause adds one step
the short opening gives the listener a fixed point
the price ends on a household, not a ledger
weaknesses: the middle sentence is near the limit of a single breath and needs a reader who can pace it
spokenRhythm: A six-word statement, a long sentence that travels inland toll by toll, and a medium line that settles on one family.
narrativeFunction: Explains why an everyday commodity became costly far from its source.
whyItWorks: A long sentence works aloud when it moves in one direction. This one follows the salt from gate to gate in order, so the listener never has to hold an earlier clause in mind to understand a later one. The short opening and the steady close frame it, and the money is measured in a labourer's wages.

text: The survey party spent forty days going up the river. They hauled the boats round every set of rapids they came to, and at the last of them they lost a boat, with most of the flour. They came back down in nine.
strengths: the short last sentence says how desperate the return was without describing it
the long middle sentence feels like the haul it describes
weaknesses: the current alone would make the return faster, so the lost flour has to carry the reason for the haste
the hunger is implied, and the next block should confirm it from the journals
spokenRhythm: A plain opener, a long laborious middle, and a six-word close that seems to rush.
narrativeFunction: Compresses an expedition's ascent and retreat into a contrast of sentence lengths.
whyItWorks: Forty days get a plain sentence, the effort gets a long one, and the retreat gets almost nothing. The listener hears the speed of the return in the rhythm before doing any arithmetic, and the lost flour, placed just before it, explains the hurry without a word about hunger.

text: The guild's rules ran to sixty-one clauses, and most of them were about quality. A cloth that failed inspection was cut in two in the market square, so that it could never be sold as a whole piece, and the weaver paid a fine for the privilege of watching. The rules said nothing at all about wages.
strengths: a medium sentence, a long one and a short one in a natural order
the dry aside sits at the end of the long sentence where the voice can lift it
the closing line reveals the guild's priorities without comment
weaknesses: for the privilege of watching is a familiar turn of phrase and should not be leaned on twice
spokenRhythm: Fourteen words, then a long sentence that carries the punishment and the joke, then a short line that changes the subject pointedly.
narrativeFunction: Describes a medieval guild's rules and quietly shows whose interests they protected.
whyItWorks: The lengths vary because the ideas vary, not because a pattern demands it. The long sentence is long because the punishment has three parts, and the short one is short because silence is its whole point. A listener hears an argument being made without the narrator stating it.

text: A beaver pelt traded at the post bought a fixed number of knives, kettles or blankets, and the price list hardly changed in thirty years. The distance did. Each decade the trappers went further north to find the animals, and the same pelt cost them a longer winter.
strengths: a three-word sentence acts as a hinge between two long ones
the real price is moved from goods to time
the last phrase is memorable and literally true
weaknesses: a hinge this short can only be used sparingly before it becomes a habit
spokenRhythm: A long steady sentence, a three-word turn, then a long sentence that resolves the turn.
narrativeFunction: Shows how the cost of the fur trade shifted onto the trappers while the official prices stayed still.
whyItWorks: The short sentence is a complete thought that the listener can hear as a turn, and it is earned by the length of the sentence before it. The final line explains the economics in human terms, and because it comes from the story it lands as a memorable line rather than a slogan.
